what: Concentra runs occupational health clinics. Its centres treat workplace injuries, conduct the physical examinations and drug tests employers require, and manage the return-to-work process — the medical services an employer needs rather than the ones a patient chooses.
customers: Employers and their workers’ compensation insurers, who pay for injury treatment, mandated physical examinations, drug screening and return-to-work certification.
money: Treatment of workplace injuries, paid by employers and their insurers.
Physical examinations, drug and alcohol testing, and return-to-work evaluations.
moat: The customer is the employer, not the patient, which changes everything: employers want an injured worker treated quickly and back at work, and they want a national network that handles it consistently across every location. Concentra has by far the largest such network in the United States, and that scale is genuinely hard to replicate clinic by clinic.
risks: Debt of $2.1B against $79.9M of cash is heavy, a legacy of the spin-off structure, and it dominates the equity value.
Revenue depends on employment levels and on industrial activity: fewer workers means fewer injuries and fewer mandated examinations.
The shares trade at about 24.5 times earnings and 15.3 times EV/EBITDA, which is full for a clinic operator.
Workers’ compensation reimbursement rates are set state by state and have been under pressure.
Ten analysts average a $47.50 target, about 15% above the current price.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $1.7B in 2022 to $2.2B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $2.3B.
Free cash flow of $257.4M on $2.3B of revenue is solid, at about 20.2 times free cash flow.
Mandated physical examinations and drug testing are legally required, not discretionary medical spending.
The national clinic network is a genuine scale advantage that a regional competitor cannot match.
Employers paying the bill want fast treatment and return to work, which aligns the incentives better than most healthcare.
watch: Patient visit volumes and revenue per visit. A clinic network is a volume business with fixed costs, so visits per clinic determines whether the economics work.
view: Concentra operates in the one corner of American healthcare where the incentives are aligned. The employer pays, and what the employer wants is an injured worker treated promptly and back at work — which is also what the worker wants and what good medicine would do anyway. Compare that with the rest of the system, where the payer wants to pay less, the provider wants to do more, and the patient wants neither bill nor delay. Alignment is rare and it is the most interesting thing about this business.

The scale advantage is real and specific. An employer with sites in thirty states does not want thirty arrangements with local clinics; it wants one national network that handles injuries, mandated examinations and drug testing consistently everywhere. Concentra has the largest such network in the country, and building a rival clinic by clinic against an incumbent that employers already use is a slow and unattractive proposition.

A meaningful part of the revenue is also legally mandated rather than chosen: certain physical examinations and drug screenings are required by regulation for particular jobs. That spending happens whether or not the economy is strong, which is a better demand characteristic than most healthcare services have. The cyclical part is injuries, which fall when employment and industrial activity fall.

At 24.5 times earnings and 15.3 times EV/EBITDA with $2.1 billion of debt against $80 million of cash, the price assumes the volume growth continues and the debt comes down. That is a lot of leverage on a business whose visit volumes move with employment, and the equity is a modest slice of the capital structure. Visit volumes and revenue per visit are the two numbers; the second one is where state-level reimbursement pressure would show up first.
bull: National network scale keeps winning multi-site employers, mandated examinations provide non-discretionary volume, and debt reduction lifts the equity.
bear: Employment and industrial activity fall so injury volumes drop, state reimbursement rates tighten, and $2.1 billion of debt magnifies it into the equity.
